claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has an inherent defect distribution and oxygen-related local lattice distortions.
The proposed multiscale framework will explicitly model spatial defect distributions, oxygen incorporation, and anharmonic phonon scattering.
The proposed model will predict electrical conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr with 1 wt.% oxygen more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal models.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies in both the approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Experimental measurements for the oxygen-containing target alloy are available or will be conducted at ambient pressure over both specified temperature regimes.
Defects and oxygen-related sites induce local lattice distortions.
Local structural and displacement disorder affects electron-scattering rates.
Lattice distortions and point defects increase phonon scattering and reduce phonon mean free paths or lattice thermal conductivity.
Electron-defect and phonon-electron interactions are the dominant mechanisms controlling the target alloy's temperature-dependent electrical conductivity.
Lattice anharmonicity is an important high-temperature conductivity mechanism in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly accounting for defect scattering and lattice anharmonicity will improve prediction accuracy.
The target alloy will exhibit nonlinear temperature dependence of electrical conductivity in the low-temperature regime.
Enhanced anharmonic effects will influence the target alloy's conductivity in the 300–1200 K regime.
Existing analytical approaches for this problem assume a perfect, defect-free crystal and neglect defect-induced scattering and anharmonic phonon contributions.
The Kubo–Greenwood formalism is an example of the conventional perfect-crystal analytical baseline.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Validity outside the stated temperature intervals or above 1 wt.% oxygen is untested.
The exact quantitative reduction in prediction error is currently undetermined and requires experimental validation.
Failure to reduce conductivity mean absolute error by at least 20% relative to a conventional perfect-crystal model in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of the predicted low-temperature nonlinearity or high-temperature anharmonic signature would falsify the hypothesis.
